summary:
"AstroEdge Health" is a local-first astronaut health-intelligence prototype designed to support crew health monitoring during deep-space missions, where communication delays can make immediate support from Earth difficult.

We developed a software platform that brings together multiple health and mission-context parameters, including SpO₂, ECG, heart rate, radiation exposure, bone-health trends and cabin environmental conditions. Its workflow combines sensor data-quality checks, individual baseline comparison, rule-based detection and experimental machine-learning capabilities to identify potential health risks and generate explainable onboard alerts. It also demonstrates local event logging and a prototype delay-tolerant data synchronization workflow.

AstroEdge Health addresses the challenge of fragmented, noisy health measurements and dependence on continuous communication with Earth by keeping monitoring and alerting local to the crew. The current prototype uses simulated sensor readings and recorded ECG data rather than live spacecraft hardware.

The project is important because it aims to improve autonomous health-risk awareness, support timely crew decisions and contribute to safer, more resilient long-duration space missions.
details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

AstroEdge Health is a local-first astronaut health-intelligence software prototype designed for deep-space missions, where communication delays can prevent astronauts from receiving immediate medical support from Earth.

The platform brings together multiple health and mission-context parameters, including:

  • SpO₂ and PPG readings
  • ECG and heart-rate information
  • Radiation exposure
  • Bone-health trends
  • Cabin environmental conditions such as oxygen, CO₂, temperature and pressure
  • Activity and mission context

Its workflow consists of four stages:

Sense: Collect health and environmental measurements from available data sources.

Validate: Check timestamps, valid ranges, signal quality, missing readings, noise and sensor faults to prevent unreliable measurements from being trusted.

Analyse: Extract useful features, compare readings against individual baselines, and apply deterministic rules alongside experimental machine-learning capabilities to identify potential health risks.

Respond: Generate categorised alerts with supporting evidence, record events locally and prepare priority data for synchronization when communication becomes available.

The core principle is that onboard monitoring and alert generation should continue independently of Earth connectivity.

2. What benefits does it provide?

  • Communication independence: Supports local health-risk monitoring during communication outages.
  • Personalised monitoring: Compares measurements against individual baseline patterns instead of relying exclusively on population-level thresholds.
  • Improved data reliability: Performs signal-quality and sensor-fault checks before analysis.
  • Explainable alerts: Provides alert severity, supporting measurements and detector information.
  • Multimodal awareness: Brings physiological, radiation, bone-health and cabin-environment information into one platform.
  • Resilient information handling: Demonstrates local event logging and a prototype store-and-forward communication workflow.

3. What is the intended impact?

The intended impact is to improve astronaut health-risk awareness and support timely onboard decision-making during long-duration space missions.

By reducing dependence on continuous communication with Earth, AstroEdge Health aims to support safer and more autonomous crew operations. Its modular architecture could also provide a foundation for future research into edge-based health monitoring, space medicine and autonomous medical-support technologies.

The system is intended to support crew awareness and medical review, not replace medical professionals, diagnose diseases or prescribe treatments.

4. What tools, programming languages and technologies were used?

Development tools

  • Visual Studio Code
  • Claude AI for AI-assisted development
  • Git and GitHub for source-code management

Frontend

  • HTML5
  • CSS3
  • JavaScript
  • Web Crypto API

Backend

  • Python
  • SQLite
  • Optional SQLCipher integration

AI and data processing

  • Rule-based detection algorithms
  • ECG and RR-interval feature processing
  • Experimental machine-learning inference architecture
  • Optional TensorFlow Lite runtime support
  • Recorded ECG data and CSV-based processing

Data security and communication

  • AES-GCM browser-side encryption
  • SHA-256 hash-based event integrity mechanism
  • JSON and CBOR data formats
  • Prototype Bundle Protocol v7 (BPv7) encoding and store-and-forward workflow

Hardware status: The current prototype is software-based. It does not yet have live wearable sensor or spacecraft hardware integration. Real-time sensor interfaces, radiation-tolerant computing hardware and hardware-in-the-loop testing are planned development stages.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creativity of AstroEdge Health lies in combining several important capabilities into one autonomous health-intelligence workflow.

Instead of treating each health parameter as an isolated measurement, the system aims to connect physiological signals, environmental conditions, radiation exposure and individual health patterns.

Its hybrid approach combines deterministic rules with experimental machine-learning capabilities, while sensor-quality validation helps prevent unreliable data from producing misleading alerts.

Another important aspect is its communication-independent design. Health monitoring and local alerting are designed to continue even when Earth communication is unavailable, while important information can be queued for later synchronization.

This combination of local-first processing, personal baselines, quality-aware analytics and explainable alerts forms the project's main system-level innovation.

6. What factors were considered during development?

The project was designed around the operational challenges of long-duration space missions:

  • Communication delays: Critical onboard monitoring must not depend on immediate communication with Earth.
  • Sensor reliability: Noisy, missing, stale or disconnected measurements must be identified.
  • Individual variation: Astronauts have different physiological baselines, so personal trends matter.
  • False alarms: Confirmation logic, signal-quality checks and explainable evidence are important for reducing alarm fatigue.
  • Resource constraints: Onboard processing, storage and communication should be efficient and predictable.
  • Privacy and security: Sensitive health information should remain protected, with controlled information sharing.
  • System resilience: Rule-based fallback and explicit fault alerts are important when a sensor or model becomes unavailable.
  • Validation and safety: Testing, hardware integration, independent medical review and mission-specific approval are necessary before operational use.

Current Development Status

AstroEdge Health is a working software prototype, not a flight-qualified or clinically validated system. The dashboard currently uses simulated sensor readings, while the ECG workflow supports recorded-data processing. The AF machine-learning component remains experimental, and real spacecraft sensor integration and full operational DTN interoperability are future development goals.

Our objective is to establish a foundation for autonomous, personalised and explainable astronaut health monitoring that can operate reliably even when Earth is far away.
